Crisis and Character — Chapter 7.
No one ever gets to choose when a crisis will hit. Sometimes, you can see it coming like a slow-building storm on the horizon. Other times, it crashes into your world out of nowhere, leaving you scrambling to regain your balance.
If you’ve ever found yourself in charge when everything’s on the line, you know: the real test isn’t just about the decisions you make—it's about the kind of person you become when the pressure is on.
Picture this: it’s early morning, and suddenly, the world seems to freeze. There’s been an international incident. The threat of conflict hangs heavy in the air, and now, all eyes are fixed on a small group of leaders. Inside the Situation Room, the tension is almost tangible. Advisors speak in careful, measured tones. New intelligence rolls in by the minute. Every option on the table feels risky.
In moments like these, the lessons you’ve learned over a lifetime really matter. Listen more than you speak. Trust your team. And above all, don’t let your ego steer the ship.
From the outside, it might look like leaders always know exactly what to do. But the truth? Doubt is always right there beside them. The best leaders are the ones who admit when they don’t have all the answers. They invite in different opinions—even the uncomfortable ones. And they refuse to let the urgency of the moment push them into making careless choices.
Sure, there’s always the temptation to make a quick decision, especially when everyone’s watching. But experience shows that patience, mixed with determination, almost always leads to better outcomes.
Once the crisis passes, the public usually just sees the final result. What they don’t see is what happened behind closed doors—the arguments, the long silences, and the bravery it took for someone to speak an inconvenient truth. Sometimes, the toughest part is knowing that no matter how carefully you choose, your decisions will have consequences—some you’ll see right away, others that might not show up for years.
Looking back, it’s clear: a crisis doesn’t create your character—it reveals it. The habits you’ve built over a lifetime—being honest, staying humble, and leading with empathy—that’s what gets you through the storm.
And when it’s all over, the most important question isn’t, “Did we win?” but, “Did we do right by the people we serve?”
